Integration of Data Driven Process Control for Maximizing Energy and Resource Efficiency in WRRFs 29 CHAPTER 5 Case Studies: Data-Driven Process Controls This chapter presents details for five case studies of data-driven process controls in real full- scale facilities for the five Applications that are the focus of this project. Collectively, these Applications provide a whole plant approach for achieving substantial energy and resource recovery benefits. Each case study includes a Background section to set the stage for the challenge that is being addressed by the data-driven process controls. Then the case study is organized by the steps used in the ML Toolkit framework (e.g., workflow): • Define Problem • Get Data • Prepare Data • Train Model • Deploy Model The case studies demonstrate in detailed, practical terms how each step of the ML Toolkit framework works such that users will have a better understanding of the workflow process and how to develop and implement ML models at their facilities. At the end of each case study, there is a Lessons Learned section which captures key learnings and guidance to help others implementing ML models to avoid unexpected challenges or reinventing the wheel. For more information on each case study, users can visit the ML Toolkit website (see Chapter 1.4) for links to the code that was used (e.g., Google Colab notebook), short project overview videos, code walk-through videos, and more. The ML models created in this project were specifically developed for implementation by the case study sites and their associated Applications; however, the approach (e.g., steps in the ML Toolkit framework) and principles used are transferrable to other WRRFs. Additionally, some relevant sections of code could potentially be utilized or incorporated into ML models at other WRRFs by trained programmers. 5.1 Carbon Diversion: High-rate Contact Stabilization (Application 1) 5.1.1 Background (Set the Stage) High-rate contact stabilization (HR-CS) is a promising high-rate bioprocess that can be used in place of or in addition to primary clarification to maximize carbon capture and energy generation. Substantial energy savings are achieved by minimizing aeration costs (minimizing carbon oxidation) and maximizing energy recovery through sidestream anaerobic digestion (methane production) (Meerburg et al. 2016). In addition to carbon and energy recovery, significant amounts of nitrogen and phosphorus (15 – 27% TN and 13 – 38% TP) are redirected to solids treatment, resulting in potential for significant reductions in energy and cost for 30 The Water Research Foundation mainstream nutrient removal and significantly enhanced sidestream nutrient recovery (Truong et al. 2020). Overall, high-rate CS systems are estimated to be able to capture 29 – 55% of influent total COD, depending on wastewater characteristics, solids retention time (SRT) applied, and degree of feast famine conditions achieved (Rahman et al 2020).
